subsection: 1. Energy requirements and the role of energy

notes.b: Energy is what the body needs to carry out all its functions, including breathing, circulating blood and moving.
points: Energy is measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal); 1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ.
The body releases energy from carbohydrate, protein, fat and alcohol through chemical reactions, and uses it for every body function.
Energy not used straight away is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles, or as fat in adipose tissue.
BMR is the minimum energy the body needs to stay alive while completely at rest.
It pays for the functions that continue at rest: breathing, the heartbeat and circulation of blood, and the work of the brain, liver, kidneys and other internal organs.
It also pays for maintaining body temperature.
BMR is measured lying completely still and awake, in a warm room, after a fast of about 12 hours.
For most people BMR is the largest single share of total daily energy use.
Age: BMR is highest during growth and falls with age, as lean muscle tissue declines.
Gender: men generally have a higher BMR than women of the same weight, because they have more lean muscle tissue and less fat.
Body size and composition: a larger body needs more energy, and lean muscle uses more energy at rest than fat tissue does.
Hormones: thyroid hormones raise BMR when they are produced in excess by an overactive thyroid gland, and lower it when the thyroid is underactive.
Activity does not change BMR itself; it changes the total energy the body uses in a day.
Energy is needed to build new body tissue, especially muscle, bone and blood.
Infants and young children need a high amount of energy for their size because they are growing quickly.
Teenagers have growth spurts with a high energy need; boys generally need more than girls at this stage.

notes.b: Physical activity is the most variable part of daily energy use, so it is the factor an individual can change most easily.
points: Energy used in activity depends on the intensity, duration and frequency of the activity.
Occupational activity: a manual worker, such as a builder or farm worker, uses far more energy than an office worker.
Leisure activity: walking, cycling, gardening and playing sport add to daily energy use.
Sedentary lifestyle: low activity means low energy output, so less food energy is needed to balance the body's needs.
Total daily energy use is made up of BMR, energy for physical activity, and energy used to digest and absorb food.
Occupation: manual and athletic work increases the requirement; sedentary work lowers it.
Climate: in cold conditions the body produces extra heat to keep its temperature stable, so energy needs rise.
Pregnancy: extra energy is needed for the growth of the baby, the placenta and the mother's extra tissue.
Lactation: extra energy is needed to make breast milk.
Health: fever, illness and recovery from injury or surgery raise energy needs; prolonged immobility lowers them.

factCards.term: Four body functions that use energy at rest
factCards.definition: Breathing; circulation of blood by the heart; activity of the brain and internal organs; maintaining body temperature.
The person lies completely still and awake in a warm room, after a fast of about 12 hours.
Age; gender; body size and lean muscle mass; thyroid hormones.

factCards.term: Two effects of a cold climate on energy needs
factCards.definition: The body produces more heat to keep its temperature stable, so energy use rises; shivering, a muscular response, also uses extra energy.

factCards.term: Two extra energy needs in pregnancy and lactation
factCards.definition: Growth of the baby, placenta and mother's extra tissue during pregnancy; production of breast milk during lactation.

factCards.term: Three main components of daily energy use
factCards.definition: BMR; energy for physical activity; energy used to digest and absorb food.

questions.prompt: Outline two factors that affect the basal metabolic rate of an adult.
questions.model: Age: BMR is highest during growth and falls with age because lean muscle tissue declines, so an older adult needs less energy at rest. Gender: men generally have a higher BMR than women of the same weight because they have more lean muscle tissue and less fat. Body size and composition, pregnancy and thyroid hormones are also accepted, with a brief explanation of how each one changes BMR.

questions.prompt: Discuss the factors that determine the total daily energy requirement of a teenager who plays competitive sport.
questions.model: BMR: a teenager has a high BMR because of growth and lean muscle development, and boys generally have a higher BMR than girls of the same weight. Growth spurts raise energy needs further. Physical activity: competitive training has high intensity, long duration and high frequency, so energy for activity is a large share of the total. Thermic effect of food: a larger amount of food eaten to meet the demand also raises the energy the body uses to digest it. Climate: training in cold or hot conditions changes the energy used to maintain body temperature. Health: illness or injury lowers activity and so reduces requirements until recovery. Intake should match these needs so that energy balance is maintained.
